claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr has improved plastic strain relative to pure tungsten.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr has improved toughness relative to pure tungsten.
Solid-solution strengthening governs the alloy's improved plastic strain and toughness.
Increased grain-boundary cohesion governs the alloy's improved plastic strain and toughness.
Multi-principal-element alloying provides solid-solution strengthening in WTaTiVZr.
Multi-principal-element alloying increases grain-boundary cohesion in WTaTiVZr.
The proposed alloying-enhanced solid-solution strengthening and grain-boundary cohesion enhance dislocation glide.
The proposed alloying-enhanced grain-boundary cohesion reduces grain-boundary embrittlement.
The material is an equimolar W-Ta-Ti-V-Zr alloy.
The controlled comparison will use high-temperature tensile and Charpy impact tests on WTaTiVZr and pure tungsten.
Tests will be conducted at 500, 700, and 900 degrees Celsius at strain rates of 10^-3 and 10^-1 s^-1.
WTaTiVZr is predicted to have higher plastic strain than pure tungsten at every specified temperature and strain rate.
WTaTiVZr is predicted to have higher toughness than pure tungsten at every specified temperature and strain rate.
The plastic-strain and toughness advantage over pure tungsten is predicted to become more pronounced as temperature increases.
The plastic-strain and toughness advantage over pure tungsten is predicted to become more pronounced as strain rate decreases.
The proposed validity domain is equimolar WTaTiVZr under high-temperature plasma-facing-component service conditions.
The proposed comparison may not isolate solid-solution strengthening from grain-boundary cohesion.
No significant plastic-strain and toughness difference from pure tungsten would falsify the hypothesis.
Characterization that does not support the predicted solid-solution-strengthening and grain-boundary-cohesion effects would falsify the hypothesis.
